Equilateral 345

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: This is a picture puzzle: a point inside an equilateral triangle sits 3, 4 and 5 steps from the three corners, and we want to know how long each side is.
How to play: Drag a corner dot or turn the dial to swing copies of the triangle around. Tick names or lengths to see them, then press Show the 60° proof.

0°
Look for the math

The surprise is that three distances measured from one point inside a triangle pin down the triangle's size. Rotate a copy of the triangle around each corner by 60°, and those distances become the sides of pieces that fit a hexagon twice as big as the triangle.

A right triangle hiding in the lengths

The numbers 3, 4 and 5 are the sides of a right triangle, because 3² + 4² = 5². By the converse of the Pythagorean theorem, any triangle with those three side lengths must have a right angle. Its area is 3 × 4 / 2 = 6. Tick show lengths on the board to see where the three distances sit.

Turning by 60 degrees

Turn the equilateral triangle by 60° around each of its corners, all in the same direction. Four copies now make one bigger equilateral triangle, with three images of P inside it. The hexagon A Pc B Pa C Pb has area twice that of ABC: the part left over is each of the triangles ABP, BCP and CAP twice. The hexagon also splits into three equilateral triangles with sides 3, 4 and 5, and three copies of the right triangle from above. The logic test checked both area sums on 175 different sizes.

Two area sums, one answer

Writing A(x) = x²√3/4 for the area of an equilateral triangle of side x, the hexagon gives
2a²√3/4 = (3² + 4² + 5²)√3/4 + 3 × (3 × 4 / 2).
That simplifies to a² = 25 + 12√3, so a ≈ 6.7664 when the distances really are 3, 4 and 5. The button sets the dial to 60°; away from 60° the copies are still turning, but they do not line up into the hexagon. The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra picture instead of the Java applet; the controls here follow the applet preserved in a 2010 Wayback snapshot. One applet quirk is kept: its FindP places P using 24 + 12√3 instead of 25 + 12√3, so its drawn distances are about 1% away from 3:4:5. The answer above is the exact one.

Set the dial to 60°, tick both boxes, then drag corner A. Watch the three coloured pieces travel with the corner while P stays put, just as in the Java applet.
